02 · RFM scoring and segment rules¶

Purpose: define Recency, Frequency and Monetary, choose the score cut-offs, turn them into the ten segment rules used for the autumn campaign, and check that the rules are stable, reproducible and easier to act on than K-Means clusters.

Production definition: sql/05_customer_rfm.sql. This notebook reads its output and the analysis marts; it does not re-run the pipeline.

TL;DR¶

  • Measures. Snapshot 2020-09-22. Recency = days since the last order; Frequency and Monetary = orders and CU spent in the trailing 365 days. 993,492 customers (73% of the 1.36M buyers) ordered in those 12 months.
  • Cut-offs. Fixed thresholds: R 30 / 60 / 120 / 180 days (365+ = Lost), F 1 / 2 / 3-4 / 5-9 / 10+ orders, M 50 / 100 / 200 / 400 CU. R and M are set near the active-customer quintiles, then moved to business periods and round amounts; F is set by hand because 34% of active customers have exactly one order, so frequency quintiles collapse into four bands and the lowest one holds 51% of customers.
  • Recency is the right main axis, but the data does not pick the cut-offs. The chance of buying again within 90 days falls smoothly with days since the last order (repeat buyers in the 2019 backtest: 78% at 0-14 days, 43% at 120-134 days, 12% at 345-359 days), with no knee anywhere.
  • Ten segments, first match wins. Champions are 14% of customers and 54% of 12-month revenue; At Risk is 89,848 customers (6.6%) with 9.5% of revenue; Lost is 27% of customers. The Python copy of the rules (used by the dashboard) matches the SQL on all 3.66M customer-snapshot rows.
  • Robust where it matters. Moving one group of cut-offs by ±25% changes Champions by 13% at most, while the narrow segments (Loyal, Slipping Regulars, At Risk) move by 38-73%. K-Means finds no natural clusters and mixes segments that need different actions, so targeting uses the rules and K-Means stays a cross-check.

Question¶

How should Recency, Frequency and Monetary be measured and cut into scores for this customer base, and which segment rules give audiences that (a) separate customers who behave differently, (b) mean the same thing every month and (c) can be typed into the CRM tool's audience builder?

Data¶

  • customer_rfm (sql/05): one row per customer and snapshot, built from fct_orders (order = one customer, one day, one channel; see notebook 01). Three snapshots with identical rules: current 2020-09-22 (targeting), backtest_seasonal 2019-09-22 and backtest_recent 2020-06-24 (validation).
  • app_customers: slim copy of the current snapshot (1,362,281 customers) used for re-scoring.
  • recency_return_curve (sql/08), rf_grid, segment_profile (sql/09), threshold_sensitivity and kmeans_* (src/rfm/analysis.py); headline numbers from reports/metrics.json.
  • Source: H&M Personalized Fashion Recommendations dataset (Kaggle, 2022). Money in CU = price × 590, gross demand (the data has no returns).

Method¶

  1. Define R, F and M at the snapshot and look at their raw distributions among 12-month-active customers.
  2. Score them two ways, quintiles (the textbook default) and fixed business thresholds, and compare.
  3. Use the backtests (same rules applied at 2019-09-22 and 2020-06-24; outcome = any order in the next 90 days) to check that recency is a sensible main axis and whether the data suggests natural cut-offs.
  4. Combine the scores into ten segments with an ordered rule list (first match wins); check sizes, Python/SQL parity and sensitivity to the cut-offs.
  5. Compare with K-Means on log R, F, M as an independent cross-check.

def show_sql(file: str, start: str, end: str, before: int = 0) -> None:
    """Print part of a SQL file: from the line containing `start` (plus `before` lines above) to the next line containing `end`."""
    lines = (get_paths().sql / file).read_text().splitlines()
    i = next(n for n, line in enumerate(lines) if start in line)
    j = next(n for n in range(i, len(lines)) if end in lines[n])
    where = f"line {j + 1}" if i - before == j else f"lines {i - before + 1}-{j + 1}"
    print(f"-- sql/{file}, {where}\n")
    print("\n".join(lines[i - before:j + 1]))


def table(df: pd.DataFrame, ints=(), pcts=(), digits: dict | None = None, pct_digits: int = 1):
    """Show a frame without its index: thousands separators, percentages, text left-aligned."""
    fmt = {c: "{:,.0f}" for c in ints} | {c: f"{{:.{pct_digits}%}}" for c in pcts} | (digits or {})
    text_cols = [c for c in df.columns if pd.api.types.is_string_dtype(df[c]) or df[c].dtype == object]
    styled = df.style.format(fmt, na_rep="-", escape="html").hide(axis="index")
    if not text_cols:
        return styled
    heads = [{"selector": f"th.col{df.columns.get_loc(c)}", "props": "text-align: left;"} for c in text_cols]
    return styled.set_properties(subset=text_cols, **{"text-align": "left"}).set_table_styles(heads, overwrite=False)

TH = Thresholds.from_config()
cust = D.mart("app_customers")
active = cust[cust.frequency_12m > 0]

Results¶

1. Definitions¶

Measure Definition at the snapshot (2020-09-22) Note
Order everything one customer bought on one day in one channel no order id in the data
Recency days since the last order (0 = bought on the snapshot day) uses the full history, so Lost customers have one too
Frequency orders in the 365 days ending on the snapshot date
Monetary CU spent in the same 365 days gross demand
Active at least one order in those 365 days the population that gets R, F and M scores
Tenure days since the first order seen in the data data starts 2018-09-20, so a lower bound

All three measures are skewed. The median active customer last ordered 85 days ago, placed 2 orders and spent 119 CU in 12 months, while the top 1% spent 1,885 CU or more. Frequency is the extreme case: 34% of active customers placed exactly one order and another 16% two, while the 11.5% with 10+ orders bring in 42% of 12-month revenue.

3. Quintiles vs fixed business thresholds¶

The textbook RFM score cuts each measure into quintiles (20% of active customers per score). The table puts the quintile cut points next to the thresholds used.

In [6]:

business = {"recency_days": "30 / 60 / 120 / 180 (365+ = Lost)", "frequency_12m": "1 / 2 / 3-4 / 5-9 / 10+",
            "monetary_12m_cu": "50 / 100 / 200 / 400"}
table(C.quantile_vs_business(edges, business))

Frequency (orders, 12m) 1 / 2 / 3 / 7 1 / 2 / 3-4 / 5-9 / 10+
Monetary (CU, 12m) 40 / 85 / 166 / 352 50 / 100 / 200 / 400
In [7]:
business_scores = score(active, TH).rename(columns={"r_score": "r", "f_score": "f", "m_score": "m"})
C.score_distribution(business_scores, "fixed business thresholds")

With the fixed thresholds every band holds between 11% and 34% of active customers: none is empty or dominant, but the bands are deliberately not equal (R2, 121-180 days, is the smallest recency band at 12%).

In [8]:
quintile_scores_ = quantile_scores(active).rename(columns={"r_q": "r", "f_q": "f", "m_q": "m"})
C.score_distribution(quintile_scores_, "quintiles")

Quintiles work for Recency and Monetary (20% each) but not for Frequency: one- and two-order customers cannot be separated by rank, so the cut points collapse, only four bands are left, nobody gets F5 and the lowest band holds 51% of active customers.

In [9]:
# The usual workaround is to rank before cutting. It restores five equal bands, but customers with the
# same number of orders then land in different scores depending only on row order.
f_ranked = pd.qcut(active.frequency_12m.rank(method="first"), 5, labels=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
orders_label = active.frequency_12m.clip(upper=5).astype(str).replace("5", "5+")
ties = pd.crosstab(orders_label, f_ranked)
ties.index.name, ties.columns.name = "orders in 12 months", "F score after ranking"
ties.style.format("{:,}")
Out[9]:
F score after ranking 1 2 3 4 5
orders in 12 months          
1 198,699 142,509 0 0 0
2 0 56,189 105,285 0 0
3 0 0 93,413 12,060 0
4 0 0 0 77,087 0
5+ 0 0 0 109,551 198,699

Ranking first gives five equal bands, but the 341,208 identical one-order customers are split 198,699 into F1 and 142,509 into F2 purely by row order, and two-order customers are split between F2 and F3. A score that depends on row order cannot be explained to the CRM team or reproduced next month.

In [10]:
# quintile cut points at each snapshot, with the same 12-month definitions
snaps = D.mart("customer_rfm", columns=["snapshot_name", "recency_days", "frequency_12m", "monetary_12m_cu"])
rows = []
for name, label in [("backtest_seasonal", "2019-09-22"), ("backtest_recent", "2020-06-24"), ("current", "2020-09-22")]:
    e = quantile_edges(snaps[snaps.snapshot_name == name])
    rows.append({"snapshot": label, **{measures[k]: " / ".join(f"{v:,.0f}" for v in vals) for k, vals in e.items()}})

Out[10]:
snapshot Recency (days since last order) Frequency (orders, 12m) Monetary (CU, 12m)
2019-09-22 26 / 65 / 119 / 233 1 / 2 / 4 / 7 40 / 85 / 172 / 376
2020-06-24 15 / 53 / 119 / 211 1 / 2 / 3 / 7 40 / 85 / 168 / 358
2020-09-22 23 / 60 / 112 / 215 1 / 2 / 3 / 7 40 / 85 / 166 / 352

Quintile edges also move with the customer base: the top recency quintile meant "last 26 days" in September 2019, "last 15 days" in June 2020 and "last 23 days" now. A fixed threshold keeps "R5 = bought in the last 30 days" true every month, so an audience built in October means the same as one built in September.

Why these numbers. The R and M cut-offs are set near the current active-customer quintiles, then moved to periods and amounts that match how the CRM team plans contacts: R 23 / 60 / 112 / 215 days → 30 / 60 / 120 / 180 (a month, two months, a season, two seasons) and M 40 / 85 / 166 / 352 CU → 50 / 100 / 200 / 400. Frequency is set by hand (1 / 2 / 3-4 / 5-9 / 10+) because its quintiles tie. 365+ days without an order = Lost, the usual 12-month-active definition. The last recency edge moves furthest (215 → 180 days), which is why R2 holds 12% of active customers rather than 20%.

4. Is recency the right main axis? The 90-day return curve¶

At each backtest date, customers are grouped in 15-day buckets by days since their last order; the curve is the share who ordered again in the following 90 days. Buckets with fewer than 500 customers are not drawn.

In [11]:
curve = D.mart("recency_return_curve")
C.return_curve(curve, "backtest_seasonal")

In the same season last year the chance of buying again falls steadily with recency, from 78% to 12% for repeat buyers and from 30% to 8% for one-time buyers, with no cliff at any of the cut-offs.

In [12]:
C.return_curve(curve, "backtest_recent")

The last-quarter backtest has the same shape, with one flat stretch at about 50% between 75 and 120 days (repeat buyers whose last order fell between late February and early April 2020, around the start of the store closure), while lapsed customers (365+ days) keep falling from 13% to 4% the longer they have been away.

In [13]:
labels = {"backtest_seasonal": "2019-09-22", "backtest_recent": "2020-06-24"}
pts = [0, 30, 60, 120, 180, 270, 345]
k = curve[curve.recency_bucket_start.isin(pts) & curve.frequency_group.isin(["2+ orders", "1 order"])].copy()
k["days since last order"] = k.recency_bucket_start.astype(str) + "-" + k.recency_bucket_end.astype(str)
k["column"] = k.snapshot_name.map(labels) + ", " + k.frequency_group
points = (k.pivot(index=["recency_bucket_start", "days since last order"], columns="column", values="return_rate_90d")
            .reset_index(level=0, drop=True)[[f"{labels[s]}, {g}" for s in labels for g in ("2+ orders", "1 order")]])

s = curve[(curve.snapshot_name == "backtest_seasonal") & (curve.frequency_group == "2+ orders")].set_index("recency_bucket_start").return_rate_90d
drops = -s.diff().dropna()
print("2019 backtest, repeat buyers:")
print(f"  average drop per 15 days, first 120 days:   {100 * (s[0] - s[120]) / 8:.1f} points")
print(f"  average drop per 15 days, 120 to 360 days:  {100 * (s[120] - s[345]) / 15:.1f} points")
print(f"  largest drop between neighbouring buckets:  {100 * drops.max():.1f} points (bucket starting at {drops.idxmax()} days)")
points.columns.name = None
points.style.format("{:.0%}")

2019 backtest, repeat buyers:
  average drop per 15 days, first 120 days:   4.3 points
  average drop per 15 days, 120 to 360 days:  2.1 points
  largest drop between neighbouring buckets:  5.4 points (bucket starting at 30 days)
Out[13]:
  2019-09-22, 2+ orders 2019-09-22, 1 order 2020-06-24, 2+ orders 2020-06-24, 1 order
days since last order        
0-14 78% 30% 75% 30%
30-44 67% 24% 63% 22%
60-74 58% 20% 51% 17%
120-134 43% 16% 47% 17%
180-194 33% 14% 39% 15%
270-284 21% 11% 29% 14%
345-359 12% 8% 20% 14%

Recency separates customers strongly and in one direction, so it is the right main axis, and frequency matters on top of it: a repeat buyer quiet for 120-134 days is still more likely to come back (43%) than a one-time buyer who ordered in the last two weeks (30%). What the curve does not do is choose the cut-offs. The steepest drop between neighbouring buckets is about 5 points, early on, and the decline then slowly flattens with no knee, so any cut-off between neighbouring buckets is defensible. The cut-offs are therefore a business choice (contact cadence and seasons), written down and kept fixed.

C.rf_heatmap(grid)

The largest single cell is R1 × F1 (one order, 181-364 days ago: 165K customers, 17% of the active base), while the recent-and-frequent cells R4-R5 × F4-F5 hold 23% of active customers.

In [16]:
C.rf_heatmap(grid, "revenue_12m_cu")

Those same R4-R5 × F4-F5 cells bring in 56.5% of 12-month revenue, R5 × F5 alone 31%: value is concentrated where recency and frequency are both high, which is the area the Champions and Loyal rules cover.

6. From scores to ten segments¶

The segments are an ordered list of rules: each customer gets the first rule they match. Scores first, then the rule list from sql/05; the value tier (12-month spend) and the 12-month channel are separate columns, not part of the segment.

In [17]:
show_sql("05_customer_rfm.sql", "-- 4. R, F, M scores", "FROM measures")

-- sql/05_customer_rfm.sql, lines 121-143

    -- 4. R, F, M scores with fixed business thresholds
    scored AS (
        SELECT
            *,
            CASE WHEN recency_days <= getvariable('r5_max_days')  THEN 5
                 WHEN recency_days <= getvariable('r4_max_days')  THEN 4
                 WHEN recency_days <= getvariable('r3_max_days')  THEN 3
                 WHEN recency_days <= getvariable('r2_max_days')  THEN 2
                 WHEN recency_days <  getvariable('lookback_days') THEN 1
                 ELSE 0 END                                                  AS r_score,
            CASE WHEN frequency_12m >= getvariable('f5_min_orders') THEN 5
                 WHEN frequency_12m >= getvariable('f4_min_orders') THEN 4
                 WHEN frequency_12m >= getvariable('f3_min_orders') THEN 3
                 WHEN frequency_12m >= getvariable('f2_min_orders') THEN 2
                 WHEN frequency_12m >= 1                            THEN 1
                 ELSE 0 END                                                  AS f_score,
            CASE WHEN frequency_12m = 0                             THEN 0
                 WHEN monetary_12m_cu >= getvariable('m5_min_cu')   THEN 5
                 WHEN monetary_12m_cu >= getvariable('m4_min_cu')   THEN 4
                 WHEN monetary_12m_cu >= getvariable('m3_min_cu')   THEN 3
                 WHEN monetary_12m_cu >= getvariable('m2_min_cu')   THEN 2
                 ELSE 1 END                                                  AS m_score
        FROM measures

        CASE
            WHEN d.is_excluded                                         THEN 'Review List'
            WHEN s.recency_days >= getvariable('lookback_days')        THEN 'Lost'
            WHEN s.tenure_days  <  getvariable('new_customer_days')    THEN 'New Customers'
            WHEN s.r_score >= 4 AND s.f_score >= 4 AND s.m_score >= 4  THEN 'Champions'
            WHEN s.r_score >= 4 AND s.f_score >= 4                     THEN 'Loyal'
            WHEN s.r_score  = 3 AND s.f_score >= 4                     THEN 'Slipping Regulars'
            WHEN s.r_score >= 4                                        THEN 'Potential Loyalists'
            WHEN s.r_score  = 3                                        THEN 'Needs Attention'
            WHEN s.f_score >= 3 OR s.m_score >= 4                      THEN 'At Risk'
            ELSE 'Hibernating'
        END                                                            AS segment,
        CASE WHEN s.frequency_12m = 0                                  THEN 'None'
             WHEN s.monetary_12m_cu >= getvariable('vip_min_cu')       THEN 'VIP'
             WHEN s.monetary_12m_cu >= getvariable('m5_min_cu')        THEN 'High'

        CASE WHEN s.frequency_12m = 0                                  THEN 'No 12m orders'
             WHEN s.store_orders_12m = 0                               THEN 'Online only'
             WHEN s.online_orders_12m = 0                              THEN 'Store only'
             ELSE 'Omnichannel' END                                    AS channel_12m,

Champions are 14% of customers but 54% of 12-month revenue (with Loyal and Slipping Regulars, 21% of customers and 67% of revenue), At Risk still carries 9.5% of revenue with 89,848 customers, and Hibernating plus Lost are almost half of all customers (48%) with 7% of 12-month revenue.

7. The Python copy of the rules gives exactly the same segments as the SQL¶

The dashboard re-segments customers live with a numpy copy of the rules (rfm.segments). If the two ever disagreed, the dashboard would show audiences the CRM tool cannot reproduce. The check re-scores every customer at all three snapshots and compares with the SQL output.

In [21]:
cols = ["snapshot_name", "recency_days", "tenure_days", "frequency_12m", "monetary_12m_cu", "is_excluded",
        "r_score", "f_score", "m_score", "segment", "value_tier"]
rfm_all = D.mart("customer_rfm", columns=cols)
rows = []
for name, df in rfm_all.groupby("snapshot_name"):
    py_scores = score(df, TH)
    py_segment = assign_segments(df, TH, py_scores).astype(str).to_numpy()
    py_tier = value_tier(df, TH).astype(str).to_numpy()
    rows.append({
        "snapshot": name, "customers": len(df),
        "score mismatches": int(sum((py_scores[c].to_numpy() != df[c].to_numpy()).sum() for c in ["r_score", "f_score", "m_score"])),
        "segment mismatches": int((py_segment != df["segment"].to_numpy()).sum()),
        "value tier mismatches": int((py_tier != df["value_tier"].to_numpy()).sum()),
    })
parity = pd.DataFrame(rows)
assert parity[["score mismatches", "segment mismatches", "value tier mismatches"]].to_numpy().sum() == 0, "Python and SQL rules disagree"
print(f"{parity.customers.sum():,} customer-snapshot rows checked, 0 mismatches")
table(parity, ints=["customers", "score mismatches", "segment mismatches", "value tier mismatches"])

3,661,241 customer-snapshot rows checked, 0 mismatches

Zero mismatches in scores, segments and value tiers on all three snapshots, so the dashboard's what-if sliders and the SQL audiences use the same rules. The same check runs as a test (tests/test_segments_parity.py).

8. How much do segment sizes depend on the exact cut-offs?¶

Each group of cut-offs (all R, all F or all M thresholds) is moved by -25% and +25%, one group at a time, and every customer is re-segmented. Lost, New Customers and the Review List are left out: they do not depend on these cut-offs.

In [22]:
sens = D.mart("threshold_sensitivity")
order = [s for s in SEGMENT_ORDER if s not in ("New Customers", "Lost", "Review List")]
variants = [f"{g} cut-offs {d}" for g in ("Recency", "Frequency", "Monetary") for d in ("-25%", "+25%")]
moves = sens.pivot(index="segment", columns="variant", values="pct_change").reindex(index=order, columns=variants)
moves.insert(0, "customers (default)", sens[sens.variant == "Default"].set_index("segment").customers.reindex(order))
moves["largest move"] = moves[variants].abs().max(axis=1)
moves = moves.rename_axis(columns=None).reset_index()
table(moves, ints=["customers (default)"], digits={v: "{:+.0%}" for v in variants} | {"largest move": "{:.0%}"})

Champions, the segment that carries most of the revenue, moves by 13% at most. Hibernating, Potential Loyalists and Needs Attention move by up to 23%, 28% and 31%, and the narrow segments move most: Slipping Regulars up to 38%, Loyal up to 62% and At Risk up to 73% (when "used to buy often" starts at 2 orders instead of 3, At Risk gains about the 65K customers that Hibernating loses). Each variant re-labels at least 26K-124K customers (2-9% of all customers), and they move between neighbouring segments rather than being reshuffled, so the order of the segments is stable, but the size of the small ones is a definition choice. That is why the thresholds are frozen, documented, and changed only with the CRM Manager's sign-off.

9. Cross-check: what does K-Means find?¶

K-Means on log-scaled, standardised R, F and M of the 992,813 active customers outside the Review List, for k = 2 to 10 (src/rfm/analysis.py).

In [24]:
km = M["kmeans"]
C.kmeans_selection(D.mart("kmeans_k_selection"), km["k_final"])

Separation is best at k = 2 (silhouette 0.44, essentially "recent vs not") and declines as k grows, with a small bump at k = 4 (0.36), the value used for the comparison: the data is a continuum rather than natural groups, so clusters slice it at boundaries nobody chose.

In [25]:
C.kmeans_crosstab(D.mart("kmeans_crosstab"), D.mart("kmeans_profile"))

The top cluster is 89% Champions, so both methods agree on who the best customers are, but the middle cluster (29% of customers, 30% of revenue) mixes At Risk (27%), Needs Attention (24%) and Slipping Regulars (17%), customers of similar value who need different actions (win-back, a nudge, a purchase-cycle reminder).

In [26]:

Decision: rules for targeting, K-Means as a sense check. The rules agree with K-Means where it matters (the best customers), but they also split the middle cluster by recency into groups with different actions. They stay put where K-Means does not: refitting the model on last quarter's data moves 4.7% of customers to another cluster although their own data has not changed. And a rule such as "last order 121-364 days ago and 3+ orders" can be typed into an audience builder, whereas a distance to a cluster centre cannot.

Limitations¶

  • The cut-offs are a judgement call. The return curve supports recency as the main axis but no data point picks 30 / 60 / 120 / 180; the sizes of the narrow segments depend on them (section 8).
  • COVID year. The 12 months to 2020-09-22 include the store closure (2020-03-20 to 2020-05-05), and 60% of today's At Risk customers last bought in March-May 2020 (reports/metrics.json). Part of their recency may reflect closed stores rather than a decision to leave, which is one reason the "do nothing" projection is re-weighted rather than read straight off the backtest (notebook 03).
  • Segments move fast. 51% of customers changed segment between 2020-06-24 and 2020-09-22, and only 68% of June's Champions were still Champions in September (20% had slipped to Slipping Regulars; reports/metrics.json, migration matrix in notebook 03). An audience extract goes stale within weeks.
  • Inputs inherit the data limits from notebook 01: orders are customer × day × channel, store purchases are only seen when the member identifies (store-heavy customers can look less frequent than they are), and Monetary is gross demand, so online-heavy customers' M scores and value tiers are likely somewhat overstated.
  • New Customers = first order in the data within the last 90 days. At the current snapshot that means no earlier order since 2018-09-20, but some may be long-lapsed customers coming back.

Recommendations / next step¶

  • Adopt the ten rules and the fixed thresholds as the segmentation spec (docs/segmentation_spec.md); change a threshold only with the CRM Manager's sign-off, and re-run the sensitivity table when proposing one.
  • Re-run sql/05 monthly and re-score audiences on campaign launch day instead of reusing an old extract.
  • Use the value tier (VIP 1,000+ CU / High 400-999 / Mid 200-399 / Low < 200) as the second axis for effort and paid reach; keep K-Means as a periodic sense check, not for targeting.
  • Next: notebooks/03_segments_and_actions.ipynb (segment profiles, the "if we do nothing" projection and the campaign plan).
